reference.source: Standard endocrinology texts and thyroid transporter disorder literature
clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder affecting boys, combining severe neurodevelopmental impairment with a characteristic thyroid function pattern
Presents with central hypotonia evolving to spasticity, profound developmental delay, and poor head control (Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome)
The hallmark biochemistry is a raised free triiodothyronine, low or low-normal free thyroxine, and normal or slightly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone
Caused by mutations in SLC16A2, encoding the MCT8 transporter that carries thyroid hormone into cells, particularly neurones
Peripheral tissues are relatively thyrotoxic while the brain is hypothyroid, so the clinical picture mixes hypermetabolic and hypothyroid features
Standard levothyroxine does not correct the neurological disease because the transporter needed to deliver hormone to neurones is defective
Diagnosis should be considered in any boy with unexplained developmental delay and this distinctive thyroid function profile
reference.pathophysiology: MCT8, encoded by SLC16A2 on the X chromosome, is a transmembrane transporter that moves thyroid hormone into cells, and it is critical for delivering hormone across the blood-brain barrier and into neurones. When it is defective, thyroid hormone cannot reach the developing brain, producing a state of cerebral hypothyroidism and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. At the same time excess hormone circulates and enters tissues that rely on other transporters, and increased peripheral conversion generates high triiodothyronine, giving a thyrotoxic effect on tissues such as muscle and driving the paradoxical thyroid function tests.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of X-linked or syndromic developmental delay with hypotonia
Thyroid hormone metabolism defects such as SBP2/SECISBP2 disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full thyroid function profile including free triiodothyronine, free thyroxine, and thyroid-stimulating hormone
Brain magnetic resonance imaging including assessment of myelination
Assessment for hypermetabolic effects such as poor weight gain and tachycardia
redFlags: Failure to thrive with a hypermetabolic state despite apparent hypothyroid features
Progressive spasticity and loss of developmental milestones
Recurrent aspiration or feeding difficulty from severe hypotonia
Misdiagnosis leading to inappropriate high-dose thyroxine that worsens thyrotoxic effects
reference.prognosis: The neurodevelopmental impairment is severe and largely irreversible, and most affected boys have profound disability; management is supportive, and experimental thyroid hormone analogues aim mainly to reduce the peripheral thyrotoxic burden rather than restore neurological function.
pitfalls: Mistaking the raised triiodothyronine for ordinary thyrotoxicosis and treating with antithyroid drugs
Giving standard levothyroxine and expecting neurological improvement
Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy labelled as cerebral palsy
Failing to recognise and manage the peripheral hypermetabolic state
references: Specialist reviews of MCT8 deficiency / Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome
management: Consider the thyroid hormone analogue tiratricol (TRIAC) to lower the peripheral thyrotoxic burden, recognising that standard levothyroxine cannot correct the neurological disease
Manage peripheral hypermetabolism with beta-blockade for tachycardia and nutritional support to counter poor weight gain
Provide supportive neurorehabilitation including physiotherapy for hypotonia and spasticity, feeding assessment and management of any seizures
Monitor thyroid function, weight, growth and cardiac status while on hormone-analogue therapy
Offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to female relatives, as this is an X-linked condition
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine, paediatric neurology and clinical genetics
